chapters.t: Here's your Briefing.
Wall Street fell again yesterday. The S&P 500 lost about one percent, the Dow one point six, and the Nasdaq slipped to its lowest level since April.

Then, after the close, Nvidia delivered. Third-quarter revenue doubled to one hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars, beating expectations. But the company also suspended shipments of its AI chips to China, and its chairman ruled out bringing back Jensen Huang as chief executive.

art.h: Nvidia Q3 Revenue Soars 103% to $115.8B, Easing AI Demand Concerns

chapters.t: In the Gulf, tensions are still rising. An ADNOC tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, with one crew member missing, and Bahrain says it intercepted new attacks from Iran overnight. Oil, meanwhile, eased as US crude stocks rose.

art.h: ADNOC Logistics Vessel Attacked in Strait of Hormuz

chapters.t: Inflation is the other theme. Euro area inflation climbed to four percent in October, and UK inflation hit three point six, both pointing to more rate hikes. In the US, the Fed's Alberto Musalem says several hikes are likely needed.
Gold slid again, to its lowest in more than a year.
Coming up: next Wednesday, the second estimate of US third-quarter GDP.
That's your Briefing. Have a good day.
Here's your Briefing.

The Gulf is the story this morning. US fighter jets struck a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says it then launched drones at a US radar system in Bahrain, and a tanker crew is reported missing in the strait.

art.h: U.S. Warplanes Strike Iranian Missile Site on Qeshm Island

chapters.t: Oil prices are rising on the attacks, even as Iraq resumes pumping crude through its pipeline to Turkey.

On Wall Street, stocks fell sharply ahead of Nvidia's quarterly results. Former chief executive Jensen Huang, who resigned last week, says he would return if the board asked. And China says it will take necessary measures after new US restrictions on chip exports.

art.h: Jensen Huang says he would be honored to return as Nvidia chief executive

chapters.t: At the Fed, New York's John Williams says the economy doesn't need a sharp rate increase, though there's still work to do on inflation.
Gold and silver have slipped to their lowest in more than a year, weighed down by a strong dollar and higher bond yields.
Coming up: US retail sales today, and next week, the second estimate of third-quarter GDP.
That's your Briefing. Have a good day.
Here's your Briefing.

Wall Street ended last week on the back foot. On Friday, the S&P 500 slipped about three-quarters of a percent, and the Nasdaq lost one point three. Tech led the way down, with data-centre equipment makers hit hardest as the AI mood cooled.
Asia had a rough end to the week too. Hong Kong fell almost three percent. And this morning, Japan reported that its economy unexpectedly shrank in the third quarter.

Oil is the story to watch. Over the weekend, Iran claimed a supertanker was sunk in the Strait of Hormuz, and Houthi forces moved closer to the Bab el-Mandeb. But this morning, prices are easing as flows through Hormuz recover.
Gold slipped below three thousand nine hundred dollars, as the Federal Reserve sounds tougher on rates.
Coming up this week: US retail sales on Tuesday, and Nvidia's earnings are getting close.

art.h: Data Center Equipment Suppliers Lose $4.2 Trillion on Fading AI Sentiment

chapters.t: That's your Briefing. Have a good day.
Here's how the week closed.
US stocks fell on Friday. The S&P 500 lost about three-quarters of a percent, the Nasdaq one point three. The Dow held almost flat.
Europe was quiet. The DAX was flat, and London's FTSE edged up a third of a percent.
Hong Kong was the weakest market, down almost three percent.
Brent crude finished flat, just under ninety-six dollars.
That's your Briefing for Friday.
Here's your Briefing.
A big day for US stocks. The S&P 500 jumped more than two percent, and the Nasdaq nearly three.
Nvidia was the exception. Its shares dropped after the company opened an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang. Rivals AMD and Broadcom rose.
Japan went the other way: the Nikkei fell almost six percent.
Oil slid nearly six percent, after the US signalled no immediate attacks on Iran.
And inflation is still running hot, keeping a Federal Reserve rate hike on the table.
That's your Briefing.
